title: Amyloid Fibers Found Crucial for Sperm Function, Scientists Reveal Unexpected Role
body:
A team of biologists has uncovered a surprising new function for amyloid‑like protein fibers that were previously thought to be confined to neurodegenerative disease. The researchers found that these fibrous structures, long recognised for their role in conditions such as Alzheimer’s, also serve as protective carriers for RNA molecules inside human sperm, ensuring the genetic material arrives intact for the earliest stages of embryonic development. The discovery reshapes our understanding of sperm biology and hints at broader, previously hidden roles for amyloid formations in normal physiology.

Sperm were once viewed as simple delivery vehicles whose sole purpose was to transport a haploid set of chromosomes to the egg. Recent work, however, has revealed that the male gamete also ferries a diverse cargo of small RNAs, including micro‑RNAs, piwi‑interacting RNAs and long non‑coding RNAs, all of which can influence gene expression after fertilisation. The new study demonstrates that many of these RNAs are packaged within or attached to amyloid‑like protein aggregates that line the sperm tail and head. Using high‑resolution microscopy, biochemical isolation, and RNA‑sequencing, the scientists showed that the fibers protect the fragile RNA strands from degradation during the arduous journey through the female reproductive tract.

The presence of amyloid structures in sperm was unexpected because amyloids are typically associated with pathological protein misfolding. Yet the team identified a specific protein, termed “sperm‑associated amyloid protein” (SAAP), that readily forms ordered β‑sheet fibrils under physiological conditions. When the researchers disrupted SAAP formation with small‑molecule inhibitors, the sperm retained normal motility but displayed a marked loss of RNA integrity and reduced capacity to support early embryonic transcription in vitro. Conversely, enhancing SAAP assembly increased the stability of the RNA payload without compromising fertilisation efficiency. These functional assays suggest that the amyloid scaffold is a deliberate, evolutionarily conserved mechanism rather than a harmful by‑product.

The findings arrive at a time when the scientific community is reassessing the broader biological roles of amyloids. Earlier studies have documented beneficial amyloid functions in bacterial biofilms, hormone storage, and even memory formation in insects. This new evidence adds mammalian reproduction to the list, underscoring the versatility of protein self‑assembly. It also prompts a re‑examination of how paternal epigenetic information is transmitted. While maternal contributions have been extensively mapped, the paternal RNA complement—and its delivery system—has remained opaque. By linking amyloid fibers to the preservation of sperm‑borne RNAs, the research opens avenues for exploring how paternal lifestyle, age, or disease might alter this protective matrix and, consequently, offspring health.

From a clinical perspective, the discovery could have far‑reaching implications. If amyloid‑mediated RNA transport proves essential for normal embryogenesis, defects in SAAP expression or function might underlie certain cases of unexplained infertility or early embryonic loss. Moreover, the ability to modulate amyloid assembly pharmacologically offers a potential strategy to improve assisted reproductive technologies. For instance, supplementing sperm preparation media with agents that stabilise SAAP fibrils could enhance the delivery of beneficial RNAs, while targeted inhibitors might be employed to prevent the transmission of harmful paternal epigenetic marks linked to disease risk.

Looking ahead, researchers plan to investigate whether similar amyloid‑RNA complexes exist in the sperm of other mammals, including livestock and model organisms, to determine the evolutionary conservation of this system. They also aim to map the specific RNA species associated with SAAP fibers and decipher how they influence gene regulatory networks after fertilisation. As the line between pathological and functional amyloids continues to blur, this breakthrough underscores the importance of revisiting long‑standing assumptions about cellular components. The humble sperm cell, once thought to be a mere DNA courier, now appears to carry a sophisticated, amyloid‑based delivery platform that could reshape our understanding of paternal contributions to the next generation.
